lesson.title: A Scattered Cloud: Recognizing No Correlation
lesson.summary: Some pairs of variables show no linear relationship at all. No correlation means the points on a scatterplot form a random looking cloud with no upward or downward trend.
lesson.body:
Not every pair of variables is related. Sometimes when you build a scatterplot, the points do not drift upward like a positive correlation and do not drift downward like the negative correlation you just studied. Instead they scatter across the graph with no consistent direction at all. This is called no correlation, and it is just as important to recognize as the other two.

Picture the difference side by side. Positive correlation: points trend up and to the right. Negative correlation: points trend down and to the right. No correlation: points are scattered with no visible trend in either direction, more like a spray of dots than a sloped cloud.

Worked example. A teacher records the shoe size and the most recent quiz score for six students:

Shoe size: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11
Quiz score: 78, 85, 70, 92, 74, 88

Read the pattern: as shoe size increases from 6 to 11, the quiz scores go 78, then up to 85, down to 70, up to 92, down to 74, then up to 88. There is no consistent rise or fall to match the steady increase in shoe size. That makes sense, because shoe size is a matter of foot growth and genetics, while quiz score depends on studying and understanding of the material. The two have no real reason to be connected, and the scatterplot confirms it.

Recognizing no correlation matters because it stops you from imagining a relationship where none exists. If you tried to force a trend line through the shoe size and quiz score data, the line would come out nearly flat, with a slope close to zero, and it would do a poor job predicting a score from a shoe size. A flat, unreliable line is a signal, not a mistake, it is telling you these two variables simply are not related.

In everyday life, no correlation is actually the most common outcome when you compare two random quantities, such as birth month and height, or a house's street number and the grade a student earns in math class. Positive and negative correlations are the interesting exceptions where a real relationship shows up. Always look at the scatterplot first, before assuming a pattern is there.
